title: What If You Burped in Space?

scenes.text: What if you burped in space? It wouldn't just be air.
On Earth, gravity lets gas rise above the food and drink in your stomach, so a burp is mostly air.
In orbit, nothing rises. Gas, liquid and food float together, like chunky bubbles, as astronaut Chris Hadfield put it.
So a burp often comes up wet. A NASA engineer called it a wet burp, closer to acid reflux.
That's why fizzy drinks are a bad idea up there: the bubbles stay mixed in and upset your stomach.
The fix? Astronaut Jim Newman pushed off a wall and burped while moving. In space, you make your own gravity.

description:
What if you burped in space? Without gravity, gas does not separate from the liquid and food in your stomach, so burps tend to bring some liquid up with them.
NASA staff describe it as a wet burp; Chris Hadfield compared the stomach contents to chunky bubbles. Astronaut Jim Newman found he could burp by pushing off a wall to create a force in place of gravity.

first_comment: Pushing off a wall works because it gives your stomach a direction for a moment. What everyday thing would you want to try in zero gravity?
